extracted.intended_audience: scholars, policymakers, and judges interested in administrative law and public administration
extracted.subtask_description: A scholarly analysis of how presidential control and administrative capacity jointly determine agencies' ability to initiate and complete rulemakings; includes conceptual definitions, empirical measures, and policy implications for courts, Congress, and the public.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presidential power components: control and capacity
rubrics_metrics.description: Presidential control is the ability to direct administrative capacity toward the President’s own policy objectives; capacity is the agency’s well-managed team of policymakers with expertise and experience necessary to implement the President’s agenda.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both control and capacity are necessary conditions for presidential policymaking success; neither alone suffices. (Original framing: 'presidential power vis-à-vis administrative policymaking has two necessary components: control and capacity.')

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of control
rubrics_metrics.description: Control is the ability to set the agency’s policymaking agenda and direct day-to-day activities of its leadership and career employees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mechanisms of control discussed include politicization of leadership, centralization of policymaking in the White House/EOP, appointments, budgeting, and regulatory review (e.g., OIRA). Empirical claims: Presidents and proxies often exercise significant influence over rulemaking agendas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of capacity (policymaking capacity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Capacity is the expertise, experience, and team production that allow agencies to choose between policy alternatives and navigate the procedural requirements of the Administrative Procedure Act (APA).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Capacity comprises substantive policy expertise, experience with the policymaking process, and effective team management; lacks of any impede rulemaking initiation and completion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variation in policymaking capacity across agencies
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies exhibit wider variation in policymaking capacity than often assumed; capacity varies substantially across federal agencies and between executive agencies and independent commissions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical evidence (survey, personnel records, rulemaking data) shows broad cross-agency differences; independent commissions often rank high on capacity because of insulation from politics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capacity's effect on rulemaking outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: Low-capacity agencies are less likely to complete rulemakings and are less likely to initiate rulemakings than high-capacity agencies, even when the President has significant control or prioritizes the rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multivariate models controlling for presidential control and priorities demonstrate the independent, substantive effect of capacity on initiation and completion rates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complementarity of control and capacity
rubrics_metrics.description: Control and capacity are complements—not substitutes: traditional markers of presidential control prove ineffective in low-capacity agencies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thus, maximal presidential control cannot substitute for managerial skill, expertise, or sufficient staffing; successful implementation requires both.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indicators of low capacity
rubrics_metrics.description: Signs that an agency lacks policymaking capacity include being overworked, under-resourced, poorly managed, losing experienced staff, and demonstrating low rulemaking completion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples in the literature include mass-adjudication crises, program backlogs, inability to respond to litigation, and empirical measures like personnel shortfalls and delayed/cancelled rulemakings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indicators of high capacity
rubrics_metrics.description: High-capacity agencies have well-managed teams, substantive expertise and experience, and institutional features (e.g., autonomy/insulation) that support effective policymaking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Independent commissions and agencies with long-standing reputations and autonomy tend to preserve capacity; management practices that recruit and retain talent bolster capacity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trade-off between capacity and control / politicization harms capacity
rubrics_metrics.description: As presidential control (politicization, centralization) increases, agencies may struggle to hire and retain expert, experienced employees, eroding administrative capacity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scholarly and empirical citations show loss of autonomy and policy discretion reduces incentives for civil servants to invest in expertise; reforms that prioritize 'responsive competence' over 'neutral competence' can weaken long-term capacity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Delegation requires agency capacity
rubrics_metrics.description: Congressional delegation presumes agencies have the capacity to exercise delegated policymaking authority; if agencies lack capacity, the virtues of delegation are undermined.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a normative criterion for evaluating when delegation is appropriate; the article urges scholars to reconsider delegation assumptions in light of capacity variation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capacity as ability to navigate APA/procedural requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Policymaking capacity includes the ability to conduct research, draft regulatory text, solicit and respond to comments, and satisfy APA procedural demands.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedural complexity (per the APA and related requirements) makes capacity a necessary precondition for lawful and durable rulemaking; references to deossification literature highlight procedural burdens.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measuring policymaking capacity
rubrics_metrics.description: Capacity can be measured using personnel records, surveys of federal executives, and rulemaking outputs (e.g., initiation and completion of rules).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article demonstrates an empirical strategy: survey federal executives, analyze 115 million personnel records, and analyze over 5,000 rulemakings to generate new measures of capacity (staffing, expertise, experience, outputs).

rubrics_metrics.name: Presidential management responsibility to build capacity
rubrics_metrics.description: Improving capacity often requires active, effective management by Presidents (creating environments for recruitment/retention), not merely increased budgets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommendations include promoting managerial competence, safeguarding reputational incentives for career staff, and balancing autonomy with oversight to attract talent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Congressional role in capacity preservation
rubrics_metrics.description: Congress should use its appropriations and oversight functions to scrutinize budget cuts and address deficits in agency capacity; failure to do so reflects weak incentives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical guidance: Congress should conduct oversight hearings and pursue long-term funding solutions; but members often lack incentives to invest in forward-looking capacity-building.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public role and electoral incentives
rubrics_metrics.description: Public awareness of agency functions and maladministration can create electoral incentives for Presidents and Congress to build capacity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Raising public awareness about agency programs and failures can press elected officials to act; absent awareness, capacity problems persist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial oversight limits and possibilities
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts are sometimes reluctant to interfere in agency resource-allocation decisions, yet may have a role policing intentional maladministration that undermines successors' powers or constitutional duties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article notes doctrinal hurdles (e.g., Heckler v. Chaney) but points to doctrines like the Take Care Clause and cases (e.g., Free Enterprise Fund) as potential avenues for judicial policing of intentional deconstruction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maladministration and intentional deconstruction as a legal and empirical concern
rubrics_metrics.description: Presidents may intentionally undermine administrative capacity (deconstruction/tie-the-hands strategies), raising questions about legal limits and remedies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Theorists (e.g., Annie Benn) model intentional undermining; courts may face difficulty distinguishing legitimate policy-driven resource choices from efforts to hobble agencies, but remedies like receivership have analogies in other constitutional contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy evaluation criterion: whether presidential control produces intended outputs
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluations of presidential influence should measure not only agenda-setting/control but actual policy outputs (e.g., rule issuance, finalization) as mediated by capacity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical work should control for both control and capacity when estimating presidential effects; measuring control alone overstates presidency's practical power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommendation: balance autonomy and oversight to sustain capacity
rubrics_metrics.description: Sustaining agency capacity requires a balance between giving civil servants some autonomy and providing sufficient oversight and managerial direction from the President, courts, Congress, and the public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy prescriptions emphasize managerial prerogatives exercised in ways that preserve expertise, morale, and reputation while maintaining accountability through oversight.
